newsitem.title: UK: Europe's Easdaq targets 30-50 firms by year-end.
newsitem.headline: Europe's Easdaq targets 30-50 firms by year-end.

text.p: Easdaq -- Europe's fledgling high-growth company stock market -- aims to have between 30 and 50 firms listed with it by the end of the year.
"We are budgeting for between 30 and 50 companies by the end of this year," Easdaq's chairman Stanislas Yassukovich told Reuters at a conference this week, adding plans were on track.

Yassukovich, a former chairman of Merrill Lynch Europe and recognised as one of the founders of the Eurobond market, said he was pleased with the way the Brussels-based market had grown since it opened last November.
"So far, so good. We are very pleased with the nature of the companies that have come forward," he said before addressing a conference on globalisation in the securities markets.
Easdaq now has eight companies listed, all "of the size, nature and quality" which Yassukovich says he had hoped for when the market was first set up.
Asked if this was in line with expectations, he said there had never been a precise target but that prospects were healthy, with a flurry of initial public offerings (IPOs) due in June.
"The rest of the pipeline is looking pretty good," he said, adding that Easdaq was aiming for companies with a market capitalisation, including the money raised, of $100 million.
Yassukovich believes the ideal company for Easdaq will not only be of this size but would also already have an international business dimension.
Such companies could, he said, benefit from the broadest community of shareholders.

He said the basic principle behind Easdaq, which Yassukovich readily admits was based on Washington-based Nasdaq, is quality not quantity and as a result for every company it agrees to process, two or three are turned away.
Most of the firms keen to join Easdaq are from France, Britain, the Netherlands, Switzerland and Austria while southern European companies were slower in expressing an interest.
But there had been indications from Italian and Spanish companies, and Germany was beginning to pick up after traditionally not having a strong equity culture, Yassukovich said.
So far the balance of Easdaq listed firms is three French, two British and two Belgian. "We are hoping it becomes a bit more diversified," he added.
The impetus for equity capital raising in Germany and other parts of Europe was being pushed forward largely by U.S. securities firms and this meant competition would be stiff.
"The creation of a competitive climate and therefore standards will be stimulated by the U.S. houses," Yassukovich said.
Easdaq aimed to provide "a single uniform standard which addresses the broadest possible range of investors in the European time zone," but is not concerned about competition from local bourses.
"We don't see a lot of competition with the national small capitalisation markets," Yassukovich said, adding that companies listed on them might migrate to Easdaq when they became larger.
Easdaq would continue to favour companies specialising in information technology and biotechnology.
